Indian Standard ON-SITE NON-MECHANICAL JOINTING OF PLIED TEXTILE REINFORCED RUBBER CONVEYOR BELTING -- CODE OF PRACTICE
PART 2 COLD VULCANIZING

FOREWORD This Indian Standard (Rut 2) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the pulleys and Belts Sectional Committee, had been approved by the Basic and Production Engineering Division Council. A standard code of practice for non-mechanical jointing of textile reinforced rubber conveyor belting at site or at place of manufacture was felt necessary to regularize practices followed in the country so long to give satisfactory quality of joints. Cold vulcanizing is useful in cases where hot vulcanizing jointing is not possible or is difficult to apply. The atmospheric conditions such as temperature, humidity and dust content should be properly controlled while doing cold vulcanizing since these are more critical than for hoi vulcanizing. Whh correct use, cold vikanizing is a ve~ successfid method of bonding raised profiles onto the finished joints of most special belts of side wall and cleated, guide strip and raised edge varieties. In preparation of this standard, considerable assistance has been derived from BS 6593:1985 `Code of practice for on-site non-mechanical jointing of plied textile and steel reinforced conveyor belting', issued by the British Standard Institution (BSI). The requirements of hot vulcanizing for on-site non-mechanical jointing of plied textile reinforced rubber conveyor belting have been covered in IS 14206 (Part 1) : 1995 `On-site non-mechanical jointing of plied textile reinforced rubber conveyor belting: Part 1 Hot vulcanizing-Code of practice'.

3.5 Plied textile reinforced rubber conveyor belting -- Fire resistant grade shall be as per IS 1891 (part 5). 4 SAFETY GUIDANCE 4.0 General The instructions and procedures given under 4.1 to 4.4 should be followed at all times during the preparation and manufacture of non-mechanical joints in conveyor belting. 4.1 Access and Power Supplies Proper means of access should be provided. If scaffolding is needed, it should be erected according to current safety practice and proper access provided. Proper lighting arrangement for working area should be made. Before starting the job, plant should be electrically isolated and where i permit to work is required, this should be obtained from the site supervisor and retained on the job. All portable equipment power supplies and plug should be compatible with the site supplies. 4.2 Jointing Material Good house-keeping should be maintained. Following precautions should be taken during handling the jointing material, used in the preparation of vulcanized joints: a) Do not work in a confined un-ventilated are% b) Avoid breathing vapors of the solvents or cleaners; c) Wear protective clothing at all time while handling vulcanizing cements and pastes; d) Avoid contact of vulcanizing solution including cement with the skin and eyes. In case of an accidental contact, treat the affected area with sufficient quantity of water. For eyes, follow the same treatment and obtain medical aid; e) Container of vulcanizing solution including cement/paste should at all time, be closed except when actually in use and smoking on the area is strictly prohibited 1

Adequate skill will only be achieved by proper training and on the job experience. 6.1.1 All operators should have sut%cient training both in the workshop and on site, followed by a period of strict on the job supervision before they are regarded as being qualtiled to carry out jointing work on site. 6.1.2 Training record should be kept and readily available for inspection. 6.2 Maintenance

MATERIAL AND EQUIPMENT

The equipment used in making joints in belting should be regularly maintained. Cutting devices should be kept sharp and any templates used should be regularly checked for dimensional accuracy.

7 TOOLS AND EQUIPMENT 7.0 General All tools, equipment and jointing material should comply with relevant Indian Standard, if available. Alternatively, the recommendation of the belt manufacturer/mdcanizing manufacturer shall be followed. 7.1 Ancillary Equipment Following equipment should be available for use: a) Two belt clamps. b) Suitable belt tensioning devices to ensure belt tightening to remove all belt sag. c) Suitable winch for stripping off the covers and plies (preferably powered winch). d) Lashing for securing structure. e) Hand tools including: i) steel tape, straight edge and square for setting out the joint; ii) hand knives for cutting: a knife specially ground to cut only through the thickness of one ply is usefid to prevent over cutting and damaging other plies; 2 clamps, etc, to the

9 JOINTING OF USED BELT 9.0 General While jointing a belt, it may be (a) New belt with new belt; (b) New belt with used belt or (c) used belt with used belt, provided that the used belts are in reasonably good conditions. In jointing the used belt (b) or (c) the precautions given under 9.1 to 9.4 should be considered to avoid defective or weak jointing. 9.1 Wet Belt Belts running in wet conditions absorb water. If this is allowed to remain in the belt during rejoining, pockets of vapour will be created within the joint area, reducing the overall strength of the joint during the running of the belt. These pockets propagate to produce larger area where adhesion is nil. Before attempting to joint such belts the prepared ends of the belts should be thoroughly dried either by natural means or by the use of electrical heater. If it is impracticable to remove the belt from the conveyor because of its size and design, it is recommended that a tempora~ shelter should be erected for d~ing the prepared ends and subsequently for jointing. 9.2 Oily and Greasy Conveyor Belt Whh some belt constructions, free oil or grease present in it will be absorbed in the belting materials thus making these belts very difficult to rejoint. Carbon tetrachloride (CCl~ may be used for cleaning the oily and greasy belt. 9.3 The Effect of Chemicals on Jointing Used Belt Many chemicals used in process industries are absorbed in belt material. These cannot be easily removed or detected. Such chemicals cause problem in belt ioint. Therefore, careful consideration should be giv& when jointing belts that have carried chemicals like, calcium chloride, calcium sulphate, sulpher dioxide, anti-foaming oils, and potash. In aJ1 such cases, advice from belt manufacturer should be sought. 9.4 Physical Condition of Used Belt Many used belts vary in thickness in their crosssection. This can be due to uneven loading, uneven wear and misalignment. When attempting to join such belt, care should be taken to ensure that the correct pressure is applied over the jointing area. Any low pressure at any thin section will lead to weak joint. 9.5 Jointing Used to New Belt When jointing 3 a new belting to used one, the

8.1 Jointing material should be obtained from a reputable supplier and should be suitably matched to the specification of the belt to be jointed. Care should be taken to ensure that shelf life is not exceeded. Following material are required for jointing: a) Cold splicing solution (capable of giving good adhesion to cotton, cotton/synthetic and synthetic fibre carcass); and b) Solvent for cleaning and swabbing : A chlorinated solvent should be preferred. Naptha, toluene or benzene may bc used. When used, this should be dried for 30 minutes to avoid residual solvent which may C:] USCblistering during vulcanization of joint. 8.2 Following information should be available on the iordainers of the material given in 8.1: a) Manufacturer's name, b) Date of manufacture, c) Material reference No., d) Shelf life, e) Instruction for use, o Storage instruction, and g) Safety instruction.

IS 14206 (Part 2) :2001

comments outlined in 9.1 to 9.4 should be adhered to in respect of oily, wet, greasy, worn and chernicaS condition when preparing the used section for vulcanizing. Particular attention should be given to (a) The difference ii thickness of the used belting with new belting, which should not exceed 1.5 mm, and (b) Compatibility in respect of belt type and strength. It is preferable that only belts with same number of plies are jointed together. If belts having different number of plies are jointed, the difference in number of plies should not exceed by one. Belts with different strength may be jointed.
10 RIGGING THE FOR JOINTLNG 10.1 Positioning BELT IN PREPARATION

b) The location should offer ease of operation for handling and positioning of a belt. c) Suitable anchorage points should be available for belt clamps and tensioning equipment. d) A reasonable working environment should be provided. e) Protection of working area from adverse weather conditions and adequate lighting arrangements should be provided wherever necessary. Steps should be taken to exclude dust and dirt from the immediate area around the joint. The joint should at all times be kept dry. 10.2 Tensioning
10.2.1 Before tensioning, any fixed take-up devices should be secured at their minimum positions and any gravity take-up devices should be in their desired final position. On inclined conveyor belt, tensioning is easier at the lower end of the conveyor.

At first the vulcanizing team should be certain that there is stilcient belting on the conveyor to complete the vulcanized joint. A suitable location for splice should be chosen and the belting should be tensioned around the conveyor in all but the joint area. A lypical conveyor arrangement is shown in Fig. 1. In selecting the most suitable location for splice, consideration for the following points should be given: a) Space should be available for suitable working table to be erected in the joint area on which to prepare the ends of the belt.

10.2.2 Belt tensioning should be done by the use of belt clamps, These should be fixed to the belt at a suitable distance from each end to allow the vulcanized joint to be completed in the area between them after the belt has been tightened by drawing them together using suitable tensioning devices. 10.2.3 The belt should be tensioned by pulling in the direction of normal travel.

11.3 Preparation of Belt Ends for Chevron Splice

The preparation of belt ends for chevron splice shall be done in the following tiner: a) Cut the two ends square. b) Mark off the centre lines on face cover of the leading end and back cover of trail end. c) Draw a base line on centre line and perpendicular to it on both ends at a distance of splice length + 50 mm from outer ends. The centrc line and base lines should be used for all future measurements. d) Mark off a point on the centre line of the leading end at a distance of 0.5 W. Joint this point with the two edge points of the base line. e) Cut the face cover and first ply along the splice line with a single ply cutter knife. Strip off the first ply and the face cover in outward direction in strip of 25 mm to 40 trim. f) Mark the centre line again and draw a point on centre line at a distance of 0.5 W (Belt width) + step length from base line. Draw two point on both edges at a distance of step length and join them with previous point. Cut the seeond ply and strip off as before. g) Repeat the operation till the last ply. h) Cut the last ply along with back cover at a length of bias length + 25 mm. j) Repeat the above operations on the trail end starting from the back cover and the bias in opposite dircctiou. 7

11.2 Preparation

of Belt Ends for Ditigonal Splice

The end which moves first during actual running is called the leading end and the other end is called the trailing end since it trails behind the leading end. The preparation of belt ends for diagonal splice shall be done in the following manner: a)
Cul

the two ends square.

b) Mark out the eeutre Iine on face cover of leading end and back cover of the trailing end by marking the mid-points of the width with the help of a measuring tape at a number of places and jointing these points with a colour pencil (preferably white). c) Mark off a base Iine over the ceutre line perpendicular to it and at a distance of total splice length + 50 mm from ends. The base line and centre line must be used for all future measurement. Draw another line parallel to 1l~ebase line 25 mtn away from it. d) MaI-k a point at one edge at a distance of bias length from second base Iinc. Join this point m the other edge of the base line. Cut through IIle first ply and face cover along the splice line using a single ply knife. Great care should

IS 14206 (Part 2) :2001 12 CLEAIWNG OF SPLICE AREA

done in the following manner: a) Paint the steps at each end of the belt with two coats of solution, ensuring that each coats properly dried before proceeding with the next operation. b) When the splice is perfectly matched turn back one half and remove the backing and then match and rolled down the splice. c) Dig in and trim off the overlapping end of last ply on the face and back to make a close fitting joint. d) Roll thoroughly the whole splice area. If necessary hammer the whole spiiced area with mallet. 14 SPLICE QUALITY Splice area should be examined for alignment and uniformity of thickness. Belt should be allowed to run at least after 4 h of completion of splice.

12.1 Cleaning of Splice Area for Synthetic Belting for Diagonal Splice

Using coarse emery cloth and wire brush, clean the surface of the ply steps without damaging the fabric and without disturbing the radish coloured dip coating of the fabric. One should remember that this coating is responsible for bonding with rubber. Any damage or removal of dip coating will lead to poor bonding and hence premature splice joint failure. 12.2 Cleaning of Sptice Area for Cotton and Cotton/ Nylon Belting for Chevron Splice Using a hand grinder and wire brush clean the surface of the ply steps without damaging the fabric. Clean the whole splice area properly. 13 JOINTING
